title: About me
text:
My research
My PhD project is about immune evasion in Merkel cell carcinoma, a rare and aggressive skin cancer. I am trying to understand why some tumours do not respond to immunotherapy.

title: About me
text:
Why this blog?
I started this blog during the course Reproducible Research in Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (September 2026). I use it as a report of what we did during the course, and a notebook I can come back to whenever I need to remember how to use the tools we learned.

title: Tuesday
text: In the morning we learned about software environments and the environment manager Pixi. In the afternoon we used Pixi on the HPC2N cluster to run a quality control (QC) of an RNA-seq dataset with FastQC, and summarised all the reports with MultiQC.

title: Tuesday
text: In the morning we learned about software environments and the environment manager Pixi. In the afternoon we used Pixi on the HPC2N cluster to run a quality control (QC) of an RNA-seq dataset with FastQC, and summarised all the reports with MultiQC.

title: Tuesday
text:
1. Why do we need environments?
It makes pipline more reproducible. Different computers have different operating systems and different versions of tools. If my FastQC version is different from yours, we might get different results.
An environment is a separate box that contains exactly the tools and versions a project needs. The tools are installed inside the environment, not on the whole computer. Each project gets its own environment, so projects never mess with each other.

title: Tuesday
text:
2. Pixi basics

Install Pixi (once per user)

wget -qO- https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
source ~/.bashrc    # reload the shell so the "pixi" command is found (on Mac: ~/.zshrc)



Create an environment

pixi init zana_pixi_training -c conda-forge -c bioconda
cd zana_pixi_training


-c adds a channel, a trusted place Pixi is allowed to download tools from.
The order matters: conda-forge first, then bioconda.

This creates a file called pixi.toml:


pixi.toml

[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]   # where tools come from
name = "zana_pixi_training"              # name of the environment
platforms = ["linux-64"]                 # operating system(s)
version = "0.1.0"

[tasks]                                  # (not used in this course)

[dependencies]                           # tools installed in the environment



Add tools and run them

pixi add quarto           # install a tool into the environment 
pixi add --help           # every command has a help page
pixi run quarto --help    # run a tool from the environment

After pixi add, a second file appears: pixi.lock. It records the exact version and source of every package.






ImportantNever delete pixi.toml or pixi.lock



Together they are the environment. pixi.toml says what I asked for, pixi.lock says exactly what was installed. Sharing these two files lets anyone rebuild the same environment.








Notepixi shell



On a normal computer, pixi shell “enters” the environment so tools can be used without typing pixi run every time (exit to leave). This does not work on HPC2N, so there I always used pixi run.

title: Tuesday
section: 3. screen: keep working when I disconnect
text:
3. screen: keep working when I disconnect
screen opens a terminal session on the server that keeps running even if my laptop goes to sleep or I lose connection.

screen -S fastqc      # start a new session called "fastqc"
# Ctrl + a, then d     -> detach (leave it running in the background)
screen -ls            # list my sessions
screen -r fastqc      # go back into the session
exit                  # inside a session: close it for good

title: Tuesday
text:
4. Setting up the project
It is important that we keep the folder organized. Raw data goes in data/, and I should never change it. Instead of copying the large files, I make symbolic links (shortcuts) to the shared course data:

mkdir -p rnaseq/data
cd rnaseq/data
ln -s /path/to/repbio26/common_data/RNAseq/*fastq.gz .
cd ..

title: Tuesday
text:
5. The FASTQ format
Sequencing reads are stored in FASTQ files. Each read takes 4 lines:

@ + the read name
the DNA sequence
a + (sometimes followed by the name again)
the quality of each base, one character per base

To look at the first reads of a (compressed) file on the server:

zcat data/SRR5223504_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8

title: Tuesday
text:
6. FastQC in a Pixi environment
FastQC is not installed on the server (fastqc: command not found), so I made an environment for it inside my project folder:

pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda
pixi add fastqc
pixi run fastqc --help


Running a job with SLURM
On a cluster, I must not run heavy work on the login node. Instead I ask the job scheduler SLURM for resources. SLURM needs to know:

-A which project pays for the computing time
-t how long the job may run (e.g. 15:00 = 15 minutes)
-n how many cores

Option 1: srun, quick, for one command:

mkdir fastqc
srun -A <project_ID> -t 15:00 -n 1 pixi run fastqc --noextract -o fastqc \
     data/SRR5223504_1.fastq.gz data/SRR5223504_2.fastq.gz

Option 2: sbatch, a script I can save and reuse. This is better for reproducibility, because the script is a record of exactly what I ran.


scripts/fastqc.sh

#! /bin/bash -l
#SBATCH -A <project_ID>
#SBATCH -t 30:00
#SBATCH -n 1

pixi run fastqc -o ../fastqc --noextract ../data/*fastq.gz


cd scripts
sbatch fastqc.sh                 # submit the job
squeue -u <username>             # check if it is waiting (PD) or running (R)
less slurm-<jobID>.out           # read the log when it's done (q to quit)

Project structure at this point:
rnaseq/
├── data/            # symbolic links to the raw fastq.gz files
├── fastqc/          # one .html + one .zip report per fastq file
├── pixi.lock
├── pixi.toml
└── scripts/
    └── fastqc.sh
To look at a report, right-click the .html file in the VS Code file explorer and choose Download.

title: Tuesday
section: 7. MultiQC: one report for all samples
text:
7. MultiQC: one report for all samples
Opening eight separate FastQC reports gets tedious. MultiQC collects them into one report.

pixi add multiqc



scripts/multiqc.sh

#! /bin/bash -l
#SBATCH -A <project_ID>
#SBATCH -t 15:00
#SBATCH -n 1

pixi run multiqc ../fastqc -o ../multiqc


sbatch multiqc.sh

The result is multiqc/multiqc_report.html.






TipReading the report



Some “failed” modules are normal for RNA-seq. For example, Per base sequence content often fails at the start of the reads because of random-primer bias, and Sequence duplication is high because highly expressed genes produce many identical reads. Always check whether a warning is expected for the type of data.

text:
Cheat sheet







I want to…
Command




create a Pixi environment
pixi init <name> -c conda-forge -c bioconda


install a tool
pixi add <tool>


run a tool
pixi run <tool> <options>


start / leave / return to screen
screen -S <name> / Ctrl+a d / screen -r <name>


link data instead of copying
ln -s /path/to/source .


peek into a fastq.gz
zcat file.fastq.gz \| head -n 8


run one command on the cluster
srun -A <proj> -t 15:00 -n 1 <command>


submit a script
sbatch script.sh


check my jobs
squeue -u <username>


check my projects
projinfo

title: Thursday
text: On Wednesday we wrote a small workflow ourselves. Today we used a ready-made, community pipeline from nf-core: nf-core/rnaseq. We ran it on our real RNA-seq data on the HPC2N cluster. Because the run takes hours, we started it inside a screen session so it kept running after we disconnected.

title: Thursday
text: On Wednesday we wrote a small workflow ourselves. Today we used a ready-made, community pipeline from nf-core: nf-core/rnaseq. We ran it on our real RNA-seq data on the HPC2N cluster. Because the run takes hours, we started it inside a screen session so it kept running after we disconnected.

title: Thursday
text:
1. What is nf-core?
nf-core is a community that builds and maintains Nextflow pipelines for common analyses (RNA-seq, variant calling, metagenomics…). Every nf-core pipeline:

is versioned (I can always rerun the exact same version, e.g. -r 3.26.0),
uses containers for every tool,
has good documentation (the Usage, Parameters and Output tabs on the website),
comes with a test profile with tiny data to check that everything works.

For publications, this makes the analysis much easier to reproduce than a homemade script.

title: Thursday
text:
2. Start a screen session first
Pipelines can run for hours. If I start them in a normal terminal and my connection drops, the run stops. So the first step is always:

screen -S rnaseq          # new session called "rnaseq"


Ctrl + a, then d: detach. The pipeline keeps running and I can close my laptop.
screen -ls: list sessions.
screen -r rnaseq: reconnect and see the progress.

title: Thursday
section: 3. Pixi environment with Nextflow and nf-core
text:
3. Pixi environment with Nextflow and nf-core

pixi init nextflow_test -c conda-forge -c bioconda
cd nextflow_test
pixi add nextflow nf-core

# check that everything works
pixi run nextflow -version
pixi run nf-core --help
pixi run nextflow run hello

title: Thursday
Thursday
section: 5. Test run with the built-in test data
text:
5. Test run with the built-in test data
Before using real data, I checked the setup and got to know the output with the pipeline’s test profile:

pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.26.0 -profile test --outdir rnaseq_test -c hpc2n.config

What each part means:







Part
Meaning




pixi run
use the Pixi environment


nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq
download and run the pipeline from nf-core


-r 3.26.0
use this exact version


-profile test
use the small built-in test data


--outdir rnaseq_test
where to save the results


-c hpc2n.config
settings for the HPC2N cluster

title: Thursday
section: 6. Running the pipeline on our RNA-seq data
text:
6. Running the pipeline on our RNA-seq data

Project folder and data

mkdir -p rnaseq_nfcore/data
cd rnaseq_nfcore
pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda
pixi add nextflow nf-core

cd data
ln -s /path/to/repbio26/common_data/RNAseq/*fastq.gz .
cd ..



The samplesheet
The pipeline needs a CSV file that lists the samples. The exact format is described in the Usage tab of the pipeline. For paired-end data it has four columns: sample name, read 1, read 2 and strandedness (auto lets the pipeline figure it out).
Instead of typing it by hand, I let a small loop write it. The chunk below runs, so you can see the result. On the server I replaced the path with my absolute path and saved it with > samplesheet.csv at the end:

DATA=/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data   # use ABSOLUTE paths

echo "sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness"
for id in SRR5223504 SRR5223517 SRR5223546 SRR5223559; do
  echo "${id},${DATA}/${id}_1.fastq.gz,${DATA}/${id}_2.fastq.gz,auto"
done

sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
SRR5223504,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223504_1.fastq.gz,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223504_2.fastq.gz,auto
SRR5223517,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223517_1.fastq.gz,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223517_2.fastq.gz,auto
SRR5223546,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223546_1.fastq.gz,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223546_2.fastq.gz,auto
SRR5223559,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223559_1.fastq.gz,/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/data/SRR5223559_2.fastq.gz,auto




Reference genome
Our samples are human. iGenomes has a human reference, but its annotation is outdated, so nf-core recommends downloading an up-to-date genome FASTA and GTF annotation (see the nf-core docs). I downloaded them to a reference/ folder.


nf-core launch → nf-params.json
On the nf-core/rnaseq page I clicked Launch version 3.26.0 and filled in the form: absolute paths to the samplesheet, the output folder, the genome FASTA and the GTF file, and resume set to true. At the end, the launcher gives a JSON file. I saved it on the server as nf-params.json and added "save_reference": true, so the genome index is saved and does not have to be built again.


nf-params.json (example, replace the paths)

{
    "input": "/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/samplesheet.csv",
    "outdir": "/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/results",
    "fasta": "/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/reference/genome.fa.gz",
    "gtf": "/path/to/rnaseq_nfcore/reference/annotation.gtf.gz",
    "save_reference": true
}







WarningJSON is picky



Every line except the last one needs a comma at the end.




Starting the run
Option A: directly with Pixi, inside the screen session. This is what I did:

screen -S rnaseq
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.26.0 -resume -params-file nf-params.json -c hpc2n.config
# Ctrl + a, d  -> detach and go home :)

Option B: submit it as a SLURM job with sbatch.


zana_submit_rnaseq.sh

#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH -A <project_ID>
#SBATCH -n 5
#SBATCH -t 24:00:00

/home/<user>/.pixi/bin/pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.26.0 \
    -params-file /path/to/nf-params.json -c /path/to/hpc2n.config


sbatch zana_submit_rnaseq.sh
squeue -u <username>

The main Nextflow process sends each step to SLURM as its own job, so squeue shows many small jobs appearing and disappearing while the pipeline runs.

title: Thursday
text:
7. The results
When the run is finished, the output folder contains, among other things:

multiqc/: the first thing to open. One report with QC, trimming, alignment and quantification statistics for all samples.
star_salmon/: alignments and the gene/transcript count tables, which are the input for differential expression analysis.
fastqc/, trimgalore/: quality control and trimming results.
pipeline_info/: exact versions of every tool and the run parameters. This is very useful for the methods section of a paper.

title: Thursday
text:
Cheat sheet







I want to…
Command




start / detach / return to a session
screen -S <name> / Ctrl+a d / screen -r <name>


set up the environment
pixi add nextflow nf-core


test a pipeline
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/<pipeline> -r <version> -profile test --outdir <dir> -c hpc2n.config


run on my data
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.26.0 -resume -params-file nf-params.json -c hpc2n.config


check jobs
squeue -u <username>


clean up old runs
nextflow log, then nextflow clean -f -before <run_name>

title: Monday
text:
Morning session was about git and git hub. In the afternoon we were setting up this blog. We will use it to make notes on everything we do during the week. The blog was createdwith Quarto, using version control with git. We uploaded it to GitHub, and set GitHub Actions so that the website is updated and published automatically every time I push changes.






TipThe idea of Reproducible Research



Someone else (or me, in six months) can take my data and my code and get the same result. So, good documentation is importnat. Quarto is a fantastic tool that lets me keep text, code and results together in one document, which is called literate programming.

title: Monday
text:
1. Creating a blog with Quarto
In VS Code, open the command palette (View → Command Palette, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + P) and type:
Quarto: Create Project
Choose Blog Project, pick a folder on your computer and give the blog a name (I gave it a name New_blog).
You can do the same thing from the terminal:

quarto create project blog New_blog


What is inside the project folder?
New_blog/
├── _quarto.yml        # settings for the whole website (title, navbar, theme...)
├── index.qmd          # the home page, which lists all posts
├── about.qmd          # the "About" page
├── profile.jpg        # picture used on the About page
├── styles.css         # extra styling 
└── posts/
    ├── _metadata.yml  # settings shared by all posts
    └── monday/
        └── index.qmd  # one folder per post, the post itself is index.qmd
Every post is in its own folder inside posts/. The home page finds them automatically. This is called a listing.

title: Monday
text:
2. Previewing the blog
To see the website while I work on it:

quarto preview

This opens the blog in the browser and refreshes it every time I save a file. In VS Code, the Preview button (top right of a .qmd file) does the same for a single page.

title: Monday
text:
3. Writing a post
A post starts with a YAML header between two lines of ---. It holds information about the post:
---
title: "Monday"
description: "One sentence shown on the home page"
date: "2026-09-14"
categories: [Quarto, git]
---
After the header comes normal text written in Markdown (**bold**, *italic*, ## Heading, [link](https://...)), and code chunks.

Code chunks
A code chunk is a block of code that Quarto can actually run when it builds the page. The result is shown right below the code.
Lines starting with #| are chunk options. They control what happens with the chunk:







Option
What it does




#| eval: false
show the code but don’t run it (I use this for code that only works on the HPC server)


#| echo: false
run the code but hide it, show only the result


#| output: false
run the code but hide the result


#| warning: false
hide warnings


#| label: my-chunk
give the chunk a name


#| fig-cap: "..."
caption for a figure









NoteWhy most chunks in this blog have eval: false



The commands from Tuesday to Thursday were run on the HPC2N server, with data and software that only exist there. My computer can’t run them, so I show the code without executing it.




Freeze
In _quarto.yml I added:
execute:
  freeze: auto
This means Quarto re-runs the code in a post only when that post has changed, and stores the results in a folder called _freeze/. I commit _freeze/ to GitHub, so GitHub Actions can build the website without needing R installed.






TipMore features



Quarto website # Here is literally everything you need to know about Quarto. It has a lot of features!

title: Monday
text:
4. Tracking the blog with git
git keeps a history of every change I make. In the terminal, inside the blog folder:

git init                      # turn the folder into a git repository
git status                    # see which files are new or changed
git add .                     # stage all files
git commit -m "Create blog"   # save a snapshot with a message

title: Monday
text:
5. Putting the blog on GitHub
On [github.com], create a new, public, empty repository (no README, no .gitignore, no license). GitHub then shows the commands under “…or push an existing repository from the command line”:

git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-REPO-NAME.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

Refresh the GitHub page and the files are there.

title: Monday
text:
6. Publishing with GitHub Actions
GitHub Pages is a free hosting service for websites. GitHub Actions is a robot that runs a set of commands every time I push. Together, they rebuild and publish the blog automatically. I followed the Quarto guide.
Step 1. Render the blog locally, so the _freeze/ folder exists:

quarto render

Step 2. Publish once by hand. This creates a branch called gh-pages, which is where the finished website lives:

quarto publish gh-pages

Step 3. On GitHub, go to Settings → Pages and check that the source is Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root).
Step 4. Add the workflow file .github/workflows/publish.yml. This is the “recipe” GitHub Actions follows:


.github/workflows/publish.yml

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: main

name: Quarto Publish

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and Publish
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

Step 5. Commit and push. The Actions tab on GitHub shows the workflow running (yellow = running, green = done, red = error). The blog will online at https://zanabrilej22.github.io/Reproducible_research_course/.

git add .
git commit -m "Add GitHub Actions workflow"
git push

From now on, every git push updates the website.






WarningDon’t push data



GitHub is for code, not data. Large files (like .fastq.gz) should be listed in .gitignore so git ignores them.

title: Wednesday
text: First we learned about containers and ran our QC tools inside them with Apptainer. Then we learned the basics of the workflow manager Nextflow and used it to build a small RNA-seq workflow (index → quantify → QC → report).

title: Wednesday
text:
Part 1: Containers

What is a container?
A Pixi environment packs the tools. A container goes one step further: it packs the tools and a whole operating system into a single file, called an image. Because the operating system travels with it, a container runs the same way on my laptop, on a colleague’s computer and on a cluster. Images do not change once they are built, so they stay stable over time.
Popular container programs are Docker, Podman and Apptainer (earlier called Singularity). On shared servers like HPC2N, Apptainer is the right choice.


Getting an image
Two good places to find images:

Docker Hub: images that people have uploaded. The biocontainers profile has many well-built bioinformatics tools.
Seqera Containers: builds an image on request from conda-forge/bioconda packages, and can put several tools into one image. Choose Singularity as the format. #we used this to get containers for Salmon, FastQC and MultiQC.


# from Seqera (note the oras:// prefix)
apptainer pull vcftools_0.1.17.sif oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/vcftools:0.1.17--b541aa8d9f9213f9

The first name (vcftools_0.1.17.sif) is what the file is called on my computer. Putting the tool name and version in it makes it clear what is inside.


Using a container

# run one command inside the container ("from the outside")
apptainer exec vcftools_0.1.17.sif vcftools --version

# open a shell inside the container ("from the inside"), type exit to leave
apptainer shell vcftools_0.1.17.sif

# make a folder from outside visible inside the container with -B outside:inside
apptainer exec -B ../data:/rawdata fastqc_0.12.1.sif ls /rawdata

exec vs run:

apptainer exec runs the command I give it. This is what I use most.
apptainer run first runs the container’s built-in runscript (its default action).



Building my own container
If nobody has made an image for a tool, I can build one from a definition file. The course example was a cow that tells the date:


lolcow.def

Bootstrap: docker
From: ubuntu:22.04

%post
    apt-get -y update
    apt-get -y install cowsay lolcat fortune

%environment
    export LC_ALL=C
    export PATH=/usr/games:$PATH

%runscript
    date | cowsay | lolcat


From: which operating system to start from
%post commands that install things
%environment settings available when the container runs
%runscript what apptainer run does


apptainer build lolcow.sif lolcow.def
apptainer run lolcow.sif



QC with containers
We repeated Tuesday’s QC, but with FastQC and MultiQC from containers instead of the Pixi environment. The only change in the SLURM script is the command line:


scripts/fastqc_container.sh

#! /bin/bash -l
#SBATCH -A <project_ID>
#SBATCH -t 30:00
#SBATCH -n 1

apptainer exec ../containers/fastqc_0.12.1.sif fastqc -o ../fastqc --noextract ../data/*fastq.gz

MultiQC from the outside and from the inside:

# outside
apptainer exec containers/multiqc.sif multiqc fastqc -o multiqc

# inside
apptainer shell containers/multiqc.sif
multiqc fastqc -o multiqc
exit

title: Wednesday
text:
Part 2: Nextflow basics

Why a workflow manager?
Nextflow:

connects the steps so the output of one becomes the input of the next,
runs independent tasks in parallel,
remembers what already finished, so I can resume after an error,
separates what to run (the workflow) from where to run it (laptop, cluster, cloud). This is called execution abstraction.



The building blocks

process: one step, e.g. “run FastQC”. It has input, output and a script.
channel: a queue that carries data from one process to the next.
workflow: the part that connects processes and channels.
executor: where the tasks run (local or slurm).






flowchart LR
    A(["greeting_ch<br/>'Hello world!'"]) --> B["SPLITLETTERS"]
    B --> C(["chunk_aa, chunk_ab"])
    C -->|flatten| D["CONVERTTOUPPER"]
    D --> E(["HELLO<br/>WORLD!"])








Setting up

screen -S nextflow
cp -r /path/to/repbio26/common_data/nf-training .
cd nf-training
pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda
pixi add nextflow



hello.nf


hello.nf

#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

params.greeting = 'Hello world!'          // a parameter I can change from the command line

process SPLITLETTERS {
    input:
    val x                                  // a value

    output:
    path 'chunk_*'                         // files starting with chunk_

    script:
    """
    printf '$x' | split -b 6 - chunk_
    """
}

process CONVERTTOUPPER {
    input:
    path y

    output:
    stdout                                 // whatever is printed

    script:
    """
    cat $y | tr '[a-z]' '[A-Z]'
    """
}

workflow {
    greeting_ch = Channel.of(params.greeting)
    letters_ch  = SPLITLETTERS(greeting_ch)
    results_ch  = CONVERTTOUPPER(letters_ch.flatten())   // flatten: one task per chunk
    results_ch.view{ it }
}


pixi run nextflow run hello.nf

Output:
executor >  local (3)
[96/fd5f07] SPLITLETTERS (1)   [100%] 1 of 1 ✔
[7e/dad424] CONVERTTOUPPER (2) [100%] 2 of 2 ✔
HELLO
WORLD!
The codes like 96/fd5f07 are the start of the folder in work/ where that task ran. It is useful for debugging. HELLO and WORLD! can come in any order because the two tasks run in parallel.


Resume and parameters

# after changing a process: only the changed part is re-run, the rest comes from the cache
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume

# change a parameter from the command line (two dashes = pipeline parameter)
pixi run nextflow run hello.nf -resume --greeting 'Bonjour le monde!'







NoteOne dash or two?



-resume has one dash, so it is an option for Nextflow itself. --greeting has two dashes, so it is a parameter of my pipeline.


Settings can come from many places. The most important ones, from strongest to weakest: command line (--param) → -params-file → -c my.config → nextflow.config in the current folder → values in the script.


Cleaning up
The work/ folder grows fast.

pixi run nextflow log                        # list previous runs in this folder
pixi run nextflow clean -f                   # remove work files
pixi run nextflow clean -before <run_name> -f

title: Wednesday
section: Part 3: A simple RNA-seq workflow with Nextflow
text:
Part 3: A simple RNA-seq workflow with Nextflow
We built this workflow step by step in script1.nf to script7.nf:





flowchart TD
    T([transcriptome.fa]) --> IDX["INDEX<br/>salmon index"]
    R([paired-end reads]) -->|fromFilePairs| RP([read pairs per sample])
    IDX --> Q["QUANTIFICATION<br/>salmon quant"]
    RP --> Q
    RP --> FQ["FASTQC"]
    Q --> M["MULTIQC"]
    FQ --> M
    M --> REP([multiqc_report.html])







INDEX: Salmon turns the transcriptome into a searchable index. This is done once.
QUANTIFICATION: for each sample, Salmon estimates how much of each transcript is present.
FASTQC: checks read quality. It runs at the same time as quantification, because neither needs the other.
MULTIQC: waits for everything and makes one report.


Running on the cluster: nextflow.config
Running on the login node is not allowed on a cluster, so we told Nextflow to send every task to SLURM. This file is read automatically when it is in the folder where I run Nextflow:


nextflow.config

process {
    executor = "slurm"
    time = '2.h'          // default time for every process
    cpus = 4

    withName: 'INDEX' {   // settings only for the INDEX process
        time = 15.m
        cpus = 2
    }
    withName: 'QUANTIFICATION' {
        time = 30.m
        cpus = 2
    }
}

resume = true             // always resume, no need to type -resume
singularity.enabled = true

executor {
    account = '<project_ID>'
}



Channels of read pairs
Salmon needs both files of a pair together. fromFilePairs groups them by sample name. The {1,2} marks the part of the file name that differs:
read_pairs_ch = channel.fromFilePairs(params.reads)
read_pairs_ch.view()
// [gut, [/.../gut_1.fq, /.../gut_2.fq]]   <- a tuple: sample ID + list of two files


The complete workflow
This is what my final script looked like. Each process gets its tool from a container, which is more reproducible than installing the tools in the environment:


script7.nf

#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

params.reads              = "$projectDir/data/ggal/gut_{1,2}.fq"
params.transcriptome_file = "$projectDir/data/ggal/transcriptome.fa"
params.outdir             = "results"

workflow {
    read_pairs_ch = channel.fromFilePairs(params.reads, checkIfExists: true)

    index_ch  = INDEX(file(params.transcriptome_file, checkIfExists: true))
    quant_ch  = QUANTIFICATION(index_ch, read_pairs_ch)
    fastqc_ch = FASTQC(read_pairs_ch)

    // mix: put both channels together; collect: wait for all and pass them as ONE item
    MULTIQC(quant_ch.mix(fastqc_ch).collect())
}

process INDEX {
    container 'oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/salmon:2.7.0--cb05356ce9eb88b7'

    input:
    path transcriptome

    output:
    path 'salmon_index'

    script:
    """
    salmon index --threads $task.cpus -t $transcriptome -i salmon_index
    """
}

process QUANTIFICATION {
    tag "Salmon on $sample_id"
    container 'oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/salmon:2.7.0--cb05356ce9eb88b7'
    publishDir "$params.outdir/salmon", mode: 'copy'

    input:
    path salmon_index
    tuple val(sample_id), path(reads)

    output:
    path "$sample_id"

    script:
    """
    salmon quant --threads $task.cpus --libType=U -i $salmon_index -1 ${reads[0]} -2 ${reads[1]} -o $sample_id
    """
}

process FASTQC {
    tag "FastQC on $sample_id"
    container '<fastqc container address from Seqera>'

    input:
    tuple val(sample_id), path(reads)

    output:
    path "fastqc_${sample_id}_logs"

    script:
    """
    mkdir fastqc_${sample_id}_logs
    fastqc -o fastqc_${sample_id}_logs -f fastq -q ${reads}
    """
}

process MULTIQC {
    container '<multiqc container address from Seqera>'
    publishDir "$params.outdir/multiqc", mode: 'copy'

    input:
    path '*'

    output:
    path 'multiqc_report.html'

    script:
    """
    multiqc .
    """
}


# run on all three samples (gut, liver, lung)
pixi run nextflow run script7.nf --reads 'data/ggal/*_{1,2}.fq'







TippublishDir and mode: 'copy'



By default, publishDir only makes links to files inside work/. If I clean work/, the results disappear. mode: 'copy' makes real copies that survive the cleanup.

title: Friday
text:
Part 1: ggplot2

Setup

install.packages("ggplot2")   # only needed once


library(ggplot2)



The grammar of graphics
Every ggplot is built from the same layers, added with +:








Layer
Question it answers
Example




data
which table?
ggplot(iris, ...)


aesthetics aes()
which column goes where (x, y, colour, size…)?
aes(x = Sepal.Length, colour = Species)


geoms
what shape? points, lines, boxes…
geom_point(), geom_boxplot()


facets
split into small panels?
facet_wrap(~ Species)


scales
how values map to colours/axes
scale_colour_manual(), scale_y_log10()


labels
titles and axis names
labs(title = ..., x = ...)


theme
the look (background, fonts…)
theme_bw()





1. A first plot
iris is a dataset built into R: flower measurements from three species.

ggplot(data = iris, mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length)) +
  geom_point()







Figure 1: The simplest ggplot: data + aesthetics + one geom.







2. Colour, labels and a theme

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Length, colour = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Petal length vs sepal length",
    x = "Sepal length (cm)",
    y = "Petal length (cm)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_bw()







Figure 2: Colour mapped to species, with labels and a cleaner theme.











ImportantInside or outside aes()?




Inside aes() = depends on the data: aes(colour = Species) gives each species its own colour.
Outside aes() = the same for everything: geom_point(colour = "blue") makes all points blue.





3. Boxplots with the data points on top

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Petal.Width, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Petal width (cm)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 3: A boxplot shows the distribution. Jittered points show every observation.







4. Facets and trend lines

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ Species) +
  theme_bw()







Figure 4: One panel per species, each with a linear trend line.







5. A volcano plot
A volcano plot is the classic way to show a differential expression result: fold change on the x-axis, significance on the y-axis. The data below is simulated, just to practise the plot.

set.seed(42)
n_genes <- 2000
de <- data.frame(
  gene   = paste0("gene_", seq_len(n_genes)),
  log2FC = rnorm(n_genes, mean = 0, sd = 1.2)
)
de$pvalue <- 10^(-abs(de$log2FC) * runif(n_genes, 0.5, 3))
de$direction <- ifelse(de$pvalue < 0.01 & de$log2FC >  1, "Up",
                ifelse(de$pvalue < 0.01 & de$log2FC < -1, "Down", "Not significant"))
head(de)

    gene     log2FC       pvalue       direction
1 gene_1  1.6451501 0.0005177275              Up
2 gene_2 -0.6776378 0.0104638682 Not significant
3 gene_3  0.4357541 0.2273419244 Not significant
4 gene_4  0.7594351 0.0100262655 Not significant
5 gene_5  0.4851220 0.5083378570 Not significant
6 gene_6 -0.1273494 0.6325646647 Not significant

table(de$direction)


           Down Not significant              Up 
            293            1444             263 



ggplot(de, aes(x = log2FC, y = -log10(pvalue), colour = direction)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.01), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Down" = "#2166ac",
                                 "Not significant" = "grey75",
                                 "Up" = "#b2182b")) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10(p-value)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 5: Volcano plot of simulated data. Dashed lines show the cut-offs |log2FC| > 1 and p < 0.01.







6. Saving a plot

p <- ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length, colour = Species)) + geom_point()
ggsave("my_plot.png", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
ggsave("my_plot.pdf", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4)   # vector format, good for papers

title: Friday
text:
Part 2: AI in bioinformatics
The afternoon was a discussion about AI in bioinformatics. The main points:
LLMs predict text, they don’t “know” things. They are trained on huge amounts of internet text, including biased and wrong content. They don’t say “I don’t know” and can hallucinate answers, including citations that don’t exist. Every reference an AI gives me must be checked.
Data privacy. Sequencing and patient data are sensitive. Pasting data into an online chatbot can send it to a company’s servers, depending on the terms of service. A safer habit is to describe the data (column names, data types) instead of uploading it. Local, open-weight models keep everything on my own computer, but need good hardware and are usually less capable.
Learning and productivity. Relying on AI too much can mean learning less. Studies discussed in the course suggest it does not always make experienced people faster either.
Responsibility. I am responsible for everything I use.
Environmental cost. Data centres use a lot of electricity and water, so it is worth thinking before sending a query.
AI and reproducibility. The habits from this week (version control, clear folder structure, documented decisions) also make it easier for an AI assistant, or a human colleague, to understand and help with a project.
